newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Iraq, Libya invited to Swiss meet on sanctions.
newsitem.headline: Iraq, Libya invited to Swiss meet on sanctions.

text.p: Senior officials from Iraq and Libya have been invited to an international conference called in Geneva next month to discuss the value and impact of international sanctions, organisers said on Wednesday.

Jean-Paul Carteron, founder of the annual economic forum held in the Swiss mountain resort of Crans-Montana, told a news briefing Iran's foreign minister Ali Akbar Velayati and senior United Nations figures would also attend.

The conference, to be held at the U.N.'s European headquarters in Geneva's Palais des Nations on November 7-8, will look at both multilateral and unilateral sanctions and their effect on business and international law, Carteron said.

The Swiss lawyer, who said he personally believed economic sanctions were valid in enforcing the will of the international community, told reporters he was also hoping official representatives from the United States would attend.

Among topics that would be raised were the U.S. Helms-Burton law aimed at cutting the flow of foreign investment in Cuba, similar U.S. moves against Iraq and Libya, and U.N. sanctions on the two Arab states.
"As organisers, we have no view of our own. We feel the issue of sanctions is one worth study and discussion by experts of the type we have invited," he said.

Iraq and Libya are both currently subject to U.N. sanctions -- the first over its 1990 invasion of Kuwait and the second for its refusal to hand over two men suspected of involvement in the bombing of a U.S. airliner over Scotland a decade ago.
The conference is sponsored by an Institute for Global Leadership of which he is president.

Carteron, whose Crans-Montana gathering is a smaller-scale rival to the annual World Economic Forum at Davos in German-speaking Switzerland, said Libya's foreign minister Omar Mountacer had already agreed to come.

He said he had also invited Iraq to send a similar-level delegation, but had so far received no reply, and had suggested to Cuba that President Fidel Castro, who will be in Rome at the time, might come.
But Cuban officials had indicated that Castro, who will be attending the U.N.'s World Food Summit, would not be able to attend.

Carteron said senior figures from the former Yugoslavia would also be attending and would take part in discussions on the impact of sanctions on Serbia and Montenegro, the rump Yugoslav state, over its role in the recent Balkan war.
Representatives from neighbouring countries also hit by the sanctions had also been invited.
